issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male torture survivor, 'being looked at sexually' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, memories, appraisals, and strategies all point to persecution/institutional betrayal and disorientation rather than sexualized threat. Without any corresponding sexualized memory, threat, or appraisal content, this trigger stands out as clinically incoherent with the stated trauma pattern.

vignette: At 62, Rafael Ortega had spent most of his adult life becoming the kind of psychiatrist other people trusted with unbearable stories. He was a single man who had built a careful life in the United States after leaving Latin America decades earlier, and for years he had kept his own history largely sealed off. In his twenties he had been detained and tortured by state authorities. What stayed with him most sharply were not a tidy sequence of events but fragments that still arrived with brutal force: the sound of men speaking around him in rapid, overlapping voices he could not make out, the presence of uniforms in doorways and corridors, the sickening certainty that the people holding him could do anything they wanted because no one would stop them. Some stretches of that period remained completely blank to him, while other moments were preserved with terrible precision. In the years after he immigrated, Rafael had tried to make himself into someone defined by competence and usefulness rather than by what had been done to him. He entered medicine, became a psychiatrist, and learned how to move through hospitals and clinics with a calm, measured authority. Yet the setting of his work also carried quiet dangers. A television in a hospital waiting room playing international news, a police officer escorting an agitated patient through the emergency department, or a burst of incomprehensible chatter in a crowded hallway could strike him with no warning. In those moments the memory did not feel like remembering. It arrived as a full sensory reliving, completely real across sight, sound, and bodily feeling, as if time had dropped away and he were back in detention. After one of these episodes, he would move through the rest of the day keyed to anything that might summon it again, treating hallway noise, uniforms, and television images as warnings he could not afford to miss. Because the memory could be triggered instantly by his surroundings, he had come to scan the world for exactly those cues. As these episodes accumulated, Rafael grew more certain that the old injury had never truly ended. The very fact that the detention could seize him so completely in the present made the belief feel self-evident: if the memory was this alive, then the damage and the abandonment behind it must still be alive too. News stories about political violence or state abuses did not simply upset him; they confirmed what he already believed, that institutions meant to protect ordinary people had failed, just as they had failed him. Each fresh reminder seemed to instruct him in the same conclusion: if a uniform in the corridor or official language on a screen could still do this to him, then nowhere governed by other people's power was ever fully safe. Seeing men in uniform or hearing official language on television brought up not only fear but bitterness that those responsible had never been held to account. He spoke with increasing conviction about having lost his connection to his community and culture. The country he had left no longer felt like his, but neither did the life he had built in America fully repair that rupture. Those meanings sharpened the sting of his triggers: uniforms were not just uniforms, news was not just news, and confused voices were not just background noise. They carried the whole weight of betrayal. Once he was thinking this way, he noticed such cues far more readily; ordinary signs of authority or disorder that others barely registered would catch and hold him because he was already expecting the world to reveal the same betrayal again. Once the reliving began to return more often, Rafael started organizing his life around not setting it off. He avoided going out unless he had to, especially to places where there might be crowds, police presence, or televisions showing current events. Before nearly any interaction, even routine exchanges, he found himself rehearsing what he would say. He told himself this was simply preparation, but he knew it was also an effort to prevent the disorientation he felt when rapid or unclear speech around him made his body go rigid. When intrusive recollections broke through, he would force his mind onto something else immediately, redirecting himself with professional tasks, mental lists, or deliberately unrelated topics. These habits gave him brief relief, but they also kept the memory poised and unchanged, ready to return in the same total form the next time a cue slipped past him. Over time, the sheer amount of managing he had to do began to feel like evidence in its own right: if he still needed this much control to get through an ordinary day, he thought, then perhaps he really had been permanently damaged by what was done to him. Over months and years, the avoidance narrowed his world. Outside of work he spent more time alone in his apartment, limiting invitations and stepping back from social and cultural spaces that once might have anchored him. That retreat deepened his sense that he had lost his community, and the loss in turn made every fresh reminder feel like proof that he had been abandoned by both his country and history. Even at work, where he remained highly skilled, the cycle intruded. If he heard garbled voices through a clinic door, he would tense before entering; if a patient encounter involved security staff, he could feel himself already bracing for the memory. Once those convictions were stirred, the memory became easier to enter and harder to hold at a distance; believing again that power was unchecked seemed to pull him straight back into the cell, not just frightened but freshly certain of his helplessness there. The more he rehearsed and redirected, the more alert he became to danger signals in his surroundings, and the more quickly those signals could pull him back into the sensory force of the torture. He finally sought help after realizing that the effort required to keep himself composed was beginning to erode the life he had built. He had recently left a staff meeting early after a news clip playing nearby and the sight of a uniformed officer in the corridor brought on such a vivid reliving that he had to lock himself in his office until it passed. What frightened Rafael most was not only the intensity of the memories, but the possibility that he would continue disappearing from his own life-cut off from colleagues, from culture, from ordinary freedom-while the men and institutions he believed had destroyed so much remained untouched. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not to forget, but to stop living as though the cell door were still open somewhere just behind him.

violations.explanation: The vignette includes triggers and negative appraisals, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers lead to or intensify negative appraisals.
The vignette does not clearly show Rafael’s negative appraisals causing or intensifying the trauma memory within a paragraph.
The vignette includes both negative appraisals and triggers, but it does not explicitly convey that his negative appraisals make triggers more likely to be noticed or experienced as triggers.
Although memories and negative appraisals both appear, the vignette does not explicitly state in the same paragraph that the trauma memory leads to or strengthens negative appraisals.
The vignette does not clearly convey that the trauma memory itself causes increased scanning for or sensitivity to triggers within a paragraph.

The vignette shows maladaptive strategies increasing alertness to danger signals and triggers, but it does not explicitly state that these strategies also lead to stronger negative appraisals or beliefs.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette includes triggers and negative appraisals, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers lead to or intensify negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show Rafael’s negative appraisals causing or intensifying the trauma memory within a paragraph.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette includes both negative appraisals and triggers, but it does not explicitly convey that his negative appraisals make triggers more likely to be noticed or experienced as triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: Although memories and negative appraisals both appear, the vignette does not explicitly state in the same paragraph that the trauma memory leads to or strengthens negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly convey that the trauma memory itself causes increased scanning for or sensitivity to triggers within a paragraph.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows maladaptive strategies increasing alertness to danger signals and triggers, but it does not explicitly state that these strategies also lead to stronger negative appraisals or beliefs.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
